newsitem.title: ESTONIA: Estonian premier formally steps down.
newsitem.headline: Estonian premier formally steps down.

text.p: Estonian Prime Minister Tiit Vaehi formally handed in his resignation on Tuesday to President Lennart Meri, two weeks after announcing he would quit.
Vaehi was forced to resign in the wake of a humiliating no-confidence vote in parliament which he only narrowly won.
The vote was prompted by allegations that Vaehi had taken part in improper privatisation of prime real estate.

"I presented my resignation to the president. Tomorrow I will present it at the Riigikogu (parliament)," Vaehi was quoted by the domestic news agency ETA as telling journalists after he left the president's palace.
Vaehi is a veteran politician and has been in power in this Baltic state since early 1995.
He had already survived two political crises, the latest of which left him in charge of a minority coalition government.
Despite political turmoil, both under Vaehi and before, Estonia has gained the reputation as a committed economic reformer since quitting the former Soviet Union in 1991.
Meri now has 14 days to name a successor to Vaehi.
The current main candidate is Mart Siiman, the head of the political faction of Vaehi's Coalition Party.
Siiman, a television and radio manager both in the Soviet and post-Soviet era, is seen as a compromise candidate that will please both the current minority coalition and the opposition.
He has already held talks with parties and believes he can gather the support of some two thirds of Estonia's 101-seat parliament, enough for him to become prime minister.
The current coalition, made up of the Coalition Party and a bloc of rural parties, commanded the firm support of 41 MPs and five or six other independents.
It is not clear whether new parties will formally join the coalition or whether they will simply back it in parliament.
Leading opposition party and Vaehi's former government partner, the Reform Party, has said it is prepared to take part in talks on joining the current minority administration.
"Siiman became a politician not long ago and presents himself as a man with the power to make decisions and solve problems," said Reform Party Secretary-General Heiki Kranich.
"He has the ability to find the best way out of a hard situation," he added.
